danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 8
paragraphs: Efter sit møde med Pierre i Moskva rejste fyrst Andrej til Petersborg, angiveligt i forretningsanliggender, men i virkeligheden for at opsøge Anatole Kurágin, som han følte det nødvendigt at stille over for. Da han nåede Petersborg, forhørte han sig om Kurágin, men denne havde allerede forladt byen. Pierre havde advaret sin svoger om, at fyrst Andrej var efter ham. Anatole Kurágin skaffede sig straks en udnævnelse fra krigsministeren og rejste til hæren i Moldavien. Mens han var i Petersborg, mødte fyrst Andrej Kutuzov, hans tidligere overgeneral, der altid havde været ham velvilligt stemt, og Kutuzov foreslog, at han skulle ledsage ham til hæren i Moldavien, hvortil den gamle general var udnævnt til øverstkommanderende. Så fyrst Andrej fik en udnævnelse ved generalstaben og rejste til Tyrkiet.

Fyrst Andrej anså det ikke for passende at skrive og udfordre Kurágin. Han mente, at hvis han udfordrede ham uden ny anledning, kunne det kompromittere den unge grevinde Rostova, og han ønskede derfor at møde Kurágin personligt for at finde et nyt påskud til en duel. Men det lykkedes ham heller ikke at møde Kurágin i Tyrkiet, for kort efter fyrst Andrejs ankomst rejste Kurágin tilbage til Rusland. I det nye land, under nye forhold, fandt fyrst Andrej livet lettere at bære. Efter at hans forlovede havde svigtet ham — hvilket han følte des smerteligere, jo mere han forsøgte at skjule virkningen — var de omgivelser, hvori han havde været lykkelig, blevet pinefulde for ham, og den frihed og uafhængighed, han engang havde skattet så højt, var det endnu mere. Han kunne ikke alene ikke længere tænke de tanker, der først var kommet til ham, da han lå og stirrede mod himlen på slagmarken ved Austerlitz, og som han senere havde uddybet med Pierre, og som havde fyldt hans ensomhed i Bogutjaróvo og derefter i Schweiz og Rom, men han frygtede endda at erindre dem og de strålende, grænseløse horisonter, de havde åbenbaret. Han beskæftigede sig nu kun med de nærmestliggende praktiske anliggender, der ikke havde forbindelse med hans tidligere interesser, og han greb dem des ivrigere, jo mere de fortidige interesser var lukket for ham. Det var, som om det ophøjede, uendelige himmelhvælv, der engang havde hvælvet sig over ham, pludselig var forvandlet til et lavt, massivt loft, der tyngede ham ned, hvori alt var klart, men intet var evigt eller hemmelighedsfuldt.

Af de virksomheder, der frembød sig for ham, var militærtjenesten den enkleste og mest velkendte. Som stabsgeneral under Kutuzov kastede han sig over arbejdet med iver og nøjagtighed og overraskede Kutuzov med sin villighed og omhu. Da han ikke havde fundet Kurágin i Tyrkiet, anså fyrst Andrej det ikke for nødvendigt at skynde sig tilbage til Rusland efter ham, men han vidste alligevel, at uanset hvor lang tid der ville gå, før han mødte Kurágin, trods sin foragt for ham og trods alle de beviser han udledte for at overbevise sig selv om, at det ikke var værd at nedlade sig til en strid med ham — vidste han, at når han mødte ham, ville han ikke kunne lade være med at udfordre ham, lige så lidt som et udsultet menneske kan lade være med at gribe efter mad. Og bevidstheden om, at fornærmelsen endnu ikke var hævnet, at hans had stadig var ubrugt, tyngede hans hjerte og forgiftede den kunstige sindsro, han formåede at opnå i Tyrkiet ved hjælp af rastløs, ihærdig og temmelig forfængelig og ærgerrig aktivitet.

I året 1812, da nyheden om krigen med Napoleon nåede Bukarest — hvor Kutuzov havde opholdt sig i to måneder og tilbragte dage og nætter med en vallakisk kvinde — bad fyrst Andrej Kutuzov om at blive forflyttet til Vestarmeen. Kutuzov, der allerede var træt af Bolkonskijs aktivitet, som syntes at bebrejde hans egen ladhed, lod ham beredvilligt rejse og gav ham en mission til Barclay de Tolly.

Inden han sluttede sig til Vestarmeen, der på det tidspunkt i maj lå i lejr ved Drissa, besøgte fyrst Andrej Kahle Bjerge, der lå direkte på hans rute, kun tre kilometer fra Smolénsk-landevejen. I de sidste tre år var der sket så mange forandringer i hans liv, han havde tænkt, følt og set så meget (på rejser både i øst og vest), at det ved ankomsten til Kahle Bjerge forekom ham mærkeligt og uventet at finde, at livet dér var uforandret og stadig det samme i enhver detalje. Han kørte ind gennem portene med stenstolperne og op ad alléen til huset, som om han trådte ind i et fortryllet, sovende slot. Den samme gamle statelighed, den samme renlighed, den samme stilhed herskede, og inde var der de samme møbler, de samme vægge, lyde og lugte og de samme ængstelige ansigter, blot lidt ældre. Prinsesse Marja (Marja) var stadig den samme sky, uanselige pige, der blev ældre, unyttigt og glædesløst tilbragte sine bedste år i frygt og stadig lidelse. Mademoiselle Bourienne var den samme koket, selvtilfredse pige, der nød hvert øjeblik af sin tilværelse og var fuld af glade forventninger til fremtiden. Hun var blot blevet mere selvsikker, syntes fyrst Andrej. Dessalles, den huslærer han havde hentet fra Schweiz, bar en frakke af russisk snit og talte gebrokkent russisk til tjenestefolkene, men var stadig den samme snævert intelligente, samvittighedsfulde og pedantiske opdrager. Den gamle fyrste (Nikolaj Andrejevitj Bolkonskij) havde kun forandret sig i udseende ved tabet af en tand, der efterlod et mærkbart hul i den ene side af munden; i karakter var han den samme som altid, blot med endnu mere irritabilitet og skepsis over for, hvad der skete i verden. Lille Nikolaj (Nikolúsjka, fyrst Andrejs søn) alene havde forandret sig. Han var vokset, blevet mere rosenkindet, havde mørkt, krøllet hår og løftede, når han var munter og lo, ganske ubevidst overfladen på sin kønne lille mund, nøjagtigt som den lille fyrstinde plejede. Han alene adlød ikke loven om uforanderlighed i det fortryllede, sovende slot. Men selv om alt ydre forblev som før, var de indre forhold mellem alle disse mennesker forandret, siden fyrst Andrej sidst havde set dem. Husholdningen var delt i to fremmede og fjendtlige lejre, som kun ændrede vaner for hans skyld og kun mødtes, fordi han var der. Til den ene lejr hørte den gamle fyrste, mademoiselle Bourienne og arkitekten; til den anden prinsesse Marja, Dessalles, lille Nikolaj og alle de gamle barnepiger og stuepiger.

Under sit ophold på Kahle Bjerge spiste hele familien sammen, men de var ilde til mode, og fyrst Andrej følte, at han var en gæst, for hvis skyld man gjorde en undtagelse, og at hans tilstedeværelse fik dem alle til at føle sig forlegne. Uvilkårligt mærkede han dette ved middagen den første dag, og han var tavs, og den gamle fyrste, der bemærkede det, blev også mørk og stum og trak sig tilbage til sine værelser umiddelbart efter middagen. Om aftenen, da fyrst Andrej gik ind til ham og for at muntre ham op begyndte at fortælle om den unge grev Kámenskijs felttog, begyndte den gamle fyrste uventet at tale om prinsesse Marja og bebrejde hende hendes overtro og hendes modvilje mod mademoiselle Bourienne, som, sagde han, var den eneste person, der virkelig var knyttet til ham.

Den gamle fyrste sagde, at hvis han var syg, var det kun på grund af prinsesse Marja: at hun med vilje bekymrede og irriterede ham, og at hun med sin overbærenhed og dumme snak forkælede lille fyrst Nikolaj. Den gamle fyrste vidste udmærket godt, at han plagede sin datter, og at hendes liv var meget hårdt, men han vidste også, at han ikke kunne lade være med at plage hende, og at hun fortjente det. »Hvorfor siger fyrst Andrej, der ser dette, ikke noget til mig om sin søster? Tror han, jeg er en skurk eller en gammel nar, der uden grund holder sin egen datter på afstand og knytter denne franske kvinde til sig? Han forstår det ikke, så jeg må forklare ham det, og han må høre på mig,« tænkte den gamle fyrste. Og han begyndte at forklare, hvorfor han ikke kunne holde ud med sin datters ufornuftige karakter.

»Hvis du spørger mig,« sagde fyrst Andrej uden at se op (han bebrejdede sin far for første gang i sit liv), »ønskede jeg ikke at tale om det, men da du spørger mig, vil jeg give dig min ærlige mening. Hvis der er nogen misforståelse eller uoverensstemmelse mellem dig og Marja, kan jeg slet ikke give hende skylden. Jeg ved, hvor højt hun elsker og ærer dig. Eftersom du spørger mig,« fortsatte fyrst Andrej, der blev irritabel, som han altid var tilbøjelig til på det seneste, »kan jeg kun sige, at hvis der er misforståelser, skyldes de denne intetsigende kvinde, som ikke er værdig til at være min søsters selskabsdame.«
Den gamle mand stirrede først stift på sin søn, og et unaturligt smil afslørede det nye hul mellem hans tænder, som fyrst Andrej ikke kunne vænne sig til.
»Hvilken selskabsdame, min kære dreng? Hvad? I har allerede talt om det! Hvad?«

»Far, jeg ønskede ikke at dømme,« sagde fyrst Andrej i en hård og bitter tone, »men du udfordrede mig, og jeg har sagt, og vil altid sige, at Marja ikke er skyld, men den skyldige — den eneste skyldige — er den franske kvinde.«

»Nå, han har fældet dom... fældet dom!« sagde den gamle mand med lav stemme og, som det forekom fyrst Andrej, med en vis forlegenhed, men så sprang han pludselig op og råbte: »Væk! Væk herfra! Lad ikke et spor af dig blive tilbage her!...«

Fyrst Andrej ville have rejst med det samme, men prinsesse Marja overtalte ham til at blive en dag endnu. Den dag så han ikke sin far, der ikke forlod sit værelse og ikke lukkede andre ind end mademoiselle Bourienne og Tíkhon, men flere gange spurgte, om hans søn var rejst. Næste dag, inden afrejsen, gik fyrst Andrej ind til sin søns værelser. Drengen, krølhåret som sin mor og strålende af sundhed, sad på hans knæ, og fyrst Andrej begyndte at fortælle ham historien om Ridder Blåskæg, men faldt hen i tanker uden at gøre historien færdig. Han tænkte ikke på dette smukke barn, sin søn, som han holdt på knæet, men på sig selv. Han søgte i sig selv enten anger over at have ophidset sin far eller sorg over for første gang i sit liv at forlade sit hjem i uvenskab med ham, og blev forfærdet over ikke at finde nogen af delene. Hvad der betød endnu mere for ham var, at han søgte og ikke fandt i sig selv den tidligere ømhed for sin søn, som han havde håbet at genopvække ved at kæle for drengen og tage ham på knæet.
»Nå, fortsæt!« sagde sønnen.
Fyrst Andrej satte ham uden et ord ned fra sit knæ og gik ud af værelset.

Så snart fyrst Andrej havde opgivet sine daglige sysler og især da han vendte tilbage til de gamle livsvilkår, midt i hvilke han havde været lykkelig, greb livslede ham med fornyet styrke, og han skyndte sig at flygte fra disse minder og finde noget arbejde så hurtigt som muligt.
»Så du har besluttet dig for at tage af sted, Andrej?« spurgte hans søster.
»Gud ske tak, at jeg kan,« svarede fyrst Andrej. »Jeg er meget ked af, at du ikke kan.«
»Hvorfor siger du det?« svarede prinsesse Marja. »Hvorfor siger du det, når du skal ud i denne forfærdelige krig, og han er så gammel? Mademoiselle Bourienne siger, han har spurgt efter dig...«
Så snart hun begyndte at tale om det, rystede hendes læber, og tårerne begyndte at strømme. Fyrst Andrej vendte sig om og begyndte at gå frem og tilbage i værelset.
»Åh, min Gud! Min Gud! Når man tænker på, hvem og hvad — hvilket skidt — der kan gøre mennesker ulykkelige!« sagde han med en ondsindethed, der forskrækkede prinsesse Marja.
Hun forstod, at han ved at tale om »skidt« ikke blot henviste til mademoiselle Bourienne, årsagen til hendes ulykke, men også til den mand, der havde ødelagt hans egen lykke.

»Andrej! Én ting beder jeg dig om, trygler dig om!« sagde hun og rørte ved hans albue, idet hun så på ham med øjne, der lyste gennem tårerne. »Jeg forstår dig« (hun slog blikket ned). »Tro ikke, at sorg er menneskers værk. Mennesker er Hans redskaber.« Hun så lidt over fyrst Andrejs hoved med det tillidsfulde, vante blik, man retter mod et sted, hvor et velkendt portræt hænger. »Sorg sendes af Ham, ikke af mennesker. Mennesker er Hans redskaber, de har ikke skylden. Hvis du mener, nogen har gjort dig uret, glem det og tilgiv! Vi har ingen ret til at straffe. Og da vil du kende lykken ved at tilgive.«

»Hvis jeg var en kvinde, ville jeg gøre det, Marja. Det er en kvindedyd. Men en mand bør ikke og kan ikke tilgive og glemme,« svarede han, og selv om han indtil da ikke havde tænkt på Kurágin, svulmede al hans ubrugte vrede pludselig op i hans hjerte.

»Hvis Marja allerede prøver at overtale mig til at tilgive, betyder det, at jeg for længst burde have straffet ham,« tænkte han. Og uden at svare hende mere begyndte han at tænke på det glade, hævngerrige øjeblik, da han ville møde Kurágin, som han vidste nu var ved hæren.

Prinsesse Marja bad ham om at blive endnu en dag og sagde, at hun vidste, hvor ulykkelig hendes far ville blive, hvis Andrej rejste uden at forlige sig med ham, men fyrst Andrej svarede, at han sandsynligvis snart ville være tilbage fra hæren og bestemt ville skrive til sin far, men at jo længere han blev nu, des mere forbitrede ville deres uoverensstemmelser blive.
»Farvel, Andrej! Husk, at ulykker kommer fra Gud, og mennesker er aldrig skyld i dem,« var de sidste ord, han hørte fra sin søster, da han tog afsked med hende.

»Så må det være sådan!« tænkte fyrst Andrej, da han kørte ud ad alléen fra huset på Kahle Bjerge. »Hun, den stakkels uskyldige skabning, er ladt tilbage som offer for en gammel mand, der har overlevet sin forstand. Den gamle mand føler, at han er skyldig, men kan ikke forandre sig. Min dreng vokser op og glæder sig over livet, hvori han som alle andre vil bedrage eller blive bedraget. Og jeg drager til hæren. Hvorfor? Det ved jeg ikke selv. Jeg vil møde den mand, som jeg foragter, for at give ham en chance til at dræbe mig og le ad mig!«

Disse livsvilkår havde været de samme før, men dengang hang de alle sammen, mens de nu alle var faldet fra hinanden. Kun meningsløse ting uden sammenhæng trængte sig den ene efter den anden ind i fyrst Andrejs sind.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: After his talk with Pierre in Moscow, Prince Andrew went to Petersburg — on business, he told his family, but really to meet Anatole Kuragin, whom he felt he had to confront. On reaching Petersburg he asked for Kuragin, but Kuragin had already left the city. Pierre had warned his brother-in-law that Prince Andrew was on his track. Anatole Kuragin promptly got an appointment from the Minister of War and went to join the army in Moldavia. While in Petersburg, Prince Andrew met Kutuzov, his former commander, who had always been well disposed toward him. Kutuzov suggested that he come along to the army in Moldavia, where the old general had just been appointed commander in chief. So Prince Andrew received a post on the headquarters staff and left for Turkey.

Prince Andrew did not think it proper to write and challenge Kuragin. He reasoned that challenging him without some fresh cause might compromise the young Countess Rostova, so he wanted to meet Kuragin in person and find a new pretext for a duel. But in Turkey too he failed to meet him, because Kuragin returned to Russia soon after Prince Andrew arrived. In a new country, amid new conditions, Prince Andrew found life easier to bear. His betrothed had broken faith with him, and the harder he tried to hide the effects, the more sharply he felt them. The surroundings where he had once been happy became painful to him, and the freedom and independence he had once prized so highly were more painful still. He could no longer think the thoughts that had first come to him as he lay gazing at the sky on the field of Austerlitz, that he had later developed with Pierre, and that had filled his solitude at Bogucharovo and then in Switzerland and Rome. He even dreaded to recall them, and the bright, boundless horizons they had opened. Now he cared only about the nearest practical matters, which had nothing to do with his past interests, and the more those past interests were closed to him, the more eagerly he seized on these. It was as if the lofty, infinite canopy of heaven that had once towered above him had suddenly turned into a low, solid vault that weighed him down — a place where everything was clear, but nothing was eternal or mysterious.

Of the activities open to him, army service was the simplest and most familiar. As a general on duty on Kutuzov's staff, he threw himself into the work with zeal and perseverance, and he surprised Kutuzov by how willing and exact he was. He had not found Kuragin in Turkey, and he did not think it necessary to rush back to Russia after him. All the same, he knew that however long it might be before they met, he would not be able to resist calling Kuragin out when they did — any more than a starving man can help snatching at food. This held despite his contempt for Kuragin and despite all the proofs he found to convince himself that stooping to a quarrel with him was not worth it. And the awareness that the insult was not yet avenged, that his rancor was still unspent, weighed on his heart. It poisoned the artificial tranquillity he managed to win in Turkey through restless, plodding, rather vainglorious and ambitious activity.

In the year 1812, news of the war with Napoleon reached Bucharest, where Kutuzov had been living for two months, spending his days and nights with a Wallachian woman. Prince Andrew asked Kutuzov to transfer him to the Western Army. Kutuzov was already weary of Bolkonski's activity, which seemed a reproach to his own idleness, and he let him go very readily, giving him a mission to Barclay de Tolly.

Before joining the Western Army, which was then, in May, encamped at Drissa, Prince Andrew visited Bald Hills. It lay directly on his way, only two miles off the Smolensk highroad. In the last three years there had been so many changes in his life, and he had thought, felt and seen so much (he had traveled in both the east and the west), that on reaching Bald Hills he found it strange and unexpected that the way of life there was unchanged, the same in every detail. He passed through the gates with their stone pillars and drove up the avenue to the house as if entering an enchanted, sleeping castle. The same old stateliness, the same cleanliness, the same stillness reigned there. Inside were the same furniture, the same walls, sounds and smell, and the same timid faces, only somewhat older. Princess Mary was still the same timid, plain maiden getting on in years, uselessly and joylessly spending the best years of her life in fear and constant suffering. Mademoiselle Bourienne was the same coquettish, self-satisfied girl, enjoying every moment of her existence and full of joyful hopes for the future. She had merely become more self-confident, Prince Andrew thought. Dessalles, the tutor he had brought from Switzerland, wore a coat of Russian cut and spoke broken Russian to the servants, but he was still the same narrowly intelligent, conscientious and pedantic teacher. The old prince had changed in appearance only by the loss of a tooth, which left a noticeable gap on one side of his mouth. In character he was the same as ever, only more irritable and more skeptical about what was happening in the world. Little Nicholas alone had changed. He had grown, filled out and turned rosy, and he had curly dark hair. When he was merry and laughing, he lifted the upper lip of his pretty little mouth quite unconsciously, just as the little princess used to do. He alone did not obey the law of immutability in the enchanted, sleeping castle. But though everything looked as it always had, the inner relations among these people had changed since Prince Andrew last saw them. The household was divided into two alien and hostile camps, who changed their habits for his sake and met only because he was there. To one camp belonged the old prince, Mademoiselle Bourienne and the architect; to the other, Princess Mary, Dessalles, little Nicholas and all the old nurses and maids.

While Prince Andrew stayed at Bald Hills, the whole family dined together, but they were ill at ease. He felt like a visitor for whose sake an exception was being made, and that his presence made everyone awkward. He felt this despite himself at dinner on the first day and kept silent. The old prince noticed it and also became morosely quiet, and he retired to his rooms right after dinner. In the evening Prince Andrew went to him and, trying to draw him out, began to tell him about the young Count Kamensky's campaign. Unexpectedly the old prince began to talk about Princess Mary. He blamed her for her superstitions and for her dislike of Mademoiselle Bourienne, who, he said, was the only person truly attached to him.

The old prince said that if he was ill, it was only because of Princess Mary: she deliberately worried and irritated him, and with her indulgence and silly talk she was spoiling little Prince Nicholas. The old prince knew very well that he tormented his daughter and that her life was very hard, but he also knew that he could not help tormenting her and that she deserved it. "Why doesn't Prince Andrew, who sees this, say anything to me about his sister? Does he take me for a scoundrel, or for an old fool who keeps his own daughter at a distance for no reason and attaches this Frenchwoman to himself? He doesn't understand, so I must explain it, and he must hear me out," thought the old prince. And he began explaining why he could not put up with his daughter's unreasonable character.

"Since you ask me," said Prince Andrew, without looking up (he was criticizing his father for the first time in his life), "I did not want to speak about it, but as you ask, I will give you my frank opinion. If there is any misunderstanding and discord between you and Mary, I can't blame her for it at all. I know how she loves and respects you. Since you ask me," Prince Andrew went on, growing irritable, as he had been liable to do lately, "I can only say that if there are any misunderstandings, they are caused by that worthless woman, who is not fit to be my sister's companion."
At first the old man stared fixedly at his son. An unnatural smile showed the fresh gap between his teeth, which Prince Andrew could not get used to.
"What companion, my dear boy? Eh? You've already been talking it over! Eh?"

"Father, I did not want to judge," said Prince Andrew in a hard, bitter tone, "but you challenged me, and I have said, and always will say, that Mary is not to blame. Those to blame — the one to blame — is that Frenchwoman."

"Ah, he has passed judgment... passed judgment!" said the old man in a low voice and, as it seemed to Prince Andrew, with some embarrassment. But then he suddenly jumped up and cried: "Be off, be off! Let not a trace of you remain here!..."

Prince Andrew wanted to leave at once, but Princess Mary persuaded him to stay another day. That day he did not see his father, who stayed in his room and admitted no one but Mademoiselle Bourienne and Tikhon, though he asked several times whether his son had gone. Next day, before leaving, Prince Andrew went to his son's rooms. The boy, curly-headed like his mother and glowing with health, sat on his knee, and Prince Andrew began telling him the story of Bluebeard, but fell into a reverie before he finished it. He was not thinking about this pretty child, his son, whom he held on his knee, but about himself. He searched himself for either remorse at having angered his father or regret at leaving home for the first time in his life on bad terms with him, and was horrified to find neither. It meant still more to him that he searched for the old tenderness for his son and did not find it, though he had hoped to reawaken it by caressing the boy and taking him on his knee.
"Well, go on!" said his son.
Prince Andrew, without replying, put him down from his knee and went out of the room.

As soon as Prince Andrew gave up his daily occupations, and especially once he was back in the old conditions of life where he had been happy, weariness of life overcame him with its former intensity. He hurried to escape from these memories and to find some work as soon as possible.
"So you've decided to go, Andrew?" asked his sister.
"Thank God that I can," replied Prince Andrew. "I am very sorry you can't."
"Why do you say that?" replied Princess Mary. "Why do you say that, when you are going off to this terrible war, and he is so old? Mademoiselle Bourienne says he has been asking about you...."
As soon as she began to speak of it, her lips trembled and her tears began to fall. Prince Andrew turned away and began pacing the room.
"Ah, my God! my God! When one thinks who and what — what trash — can cause people misery!" he said, with a malignity that alarmed Princess Mary.
She understood that by "trash" he meant not only Mademoiselle Bourienne, the cause of her misery, but also the man who had ruined his own happiness.

"Andrew! There is one thing I beg, I entreat of you!" she said, touching his elbow and looking at him with eyes that shone through her tears. "I understand you" (she looked down). "Don't imagine that sorrow is the work of men. Men are His tools." She looked a little above Prince Andrew's head, with the confident, habitual look with which one looks at the place where a familiar portrait hangs. "Sorrow is sent by Him, not by men. Men are His instruments; they are not to blame. If you think someone has wronged you, forget it and forgive! We have no right to punish. And then you will know the happiness of forgiving."

"If I were a woman I would do so, Mary. That is a woman's virtue. But a man should not and cannot forgive and forget," he replied. Until that moment he had not been thinking of Kuragin, but now all his unspent anger suddenly swelled up in his heart.

"If Mary is already urging me to forgive, it means I ought to have punished him long ago," he thought. And without answering her further, he began to think of the glad, vindictive moment when he would meet Kuragin, who he knew was now in the army.

Princess Mary begged him to stay one day more. She said she knew how unhappy her father would be if Andrew left without being reconciled to him. But Prince Andrew replied that he would probably be back from the army soon and would certainly write to his father, and that the longer he stayed now, the more bitter their differences would become.
"Good-by, Andrew! Remember that misfortunes come from God, and men are never to blame," were the last words he heard from his sister as he took leave of her.

"Then it must be so!" thought Prince Andrew as he drove out of the avenue from the house at Bald Hills. "She, poor innocent creature, is left to be victimized by an old man who has outlived his wits. The old man feels he is guilty but cannot change himself. My boy is growing up and rejoicing in life, in which, like everybody else, he will deceive or be deceived. And I am off to the army. Why? I don't know myself. I want to meet that man whom I despise, to give him a chance to kill me and laugh at me!"

These conditions of life had been the same before, but then they had all been connected; now they had all tumbled to pieces. Only senseless things, lacking coherence, presented themselves one after another to Prince Andrew's mind.
